stair-treads.title: Stair Treads Sarasota FL | Stair Remodel & Install
stair-treads.description: Hardwood, LVP and laminate stair treads matched to the field floor, installed to Florida code in Sarasota and Manatee County. 2026 pricing from $55 per tread.
stair-treads.h1: Stair Tread Installation and Remodels in Sarasota and Manatee County
stair-treads.lede: A staircase takes more daily wear than almost any other surface in the house, and matching material to the field floor is only half the job.
stair-treads.capsule: Stair tread installation and remodels in Sarasota and Manatee County cover solid hardwood, engineered hardwood, LVP and laminate treads matched to your existing or new field floor. 2026 installed pricing runs $55 to $220 per tread depending on material, plus $25 to $65 per riser. Most full staircases of 14 to 22 steps finish in two days.
stair-treads.near_me_html: Stair remodel near me calls come mostly from two-story homes, and that's concentrated in the newer-construction communities: Lakewood Ranch, Parrish, Palmetto and Bradenton inland, Venice and Wellen Park to the south. Builder-grade staircases in those subdivisions are almost always carpeted pine, which is usually the first thing homeowners replace once the field floor downstairs is done. Palmetto and Bradenton stair jobs typically pair with a full downstairs flooring replacement happening the same week, since both projects need the house cleared of furniture anyway. See our Lakewood Ranch stair treads page for specifics on that market.

sections.h2: Tread options and what holds up on a staircase
sections.html:
A staircase sees more concentrated wear per square foot than any floor in the house, which changes which materials make sense compared to the field floor they're matched to.

MaterialInstalled range per treadDurability notesBest for
Solid hardwood$130-$220Sandable up to 8 times over its lifeMatching solid field floors, formal staircases
Engineered hardwood$110-$180Wear layer limits future sandingMatching engineered field floors on slab homes
LVP$65-$105Fully waterproof, glued rather than floatedMatching LVP field floors, rental properties
Laminate$55-$85Not water-resistant on open stair edgesMatching laminate field floors, budget remodels
Risers$25-$65Painted, stained or openAny material combination above

We glue every LVP and laminate tread rather than floating it, because a floating plank has nowhere to lock against on an open stair edge the way it does surrounded by other planks on a flat floor. Solid and engineered hardwood treads get nailed and glued to the stringer the same way a traditional staircase always has. Tread and riser pricing scales with species and finish complexity more than with staircase length: a straight run of 14 open-tread steps in solid oak costs meaningfully less per step than the same 14 steps with a curved winder section, painted risers, and a custom stain match to an existing floor. Our blog post on what hardwood stair treads cost breaks the per-step math down further.

Florida Residential Code sets nosing projection at 3/4 inch to 1-1/4 inch on stairs with solid risers, and we fabricate every tread's nosing to fall inside that range rather than defaulting to whatever profile is easiest to cut. Bullnose, square and beveled are the three profiles we install most; bullnose is the traditional look for hardwood, while square-edge nosing tends to match cleaner against an LVP or laminate field floor.

The same code section sets riser and tread dimensions for the staircase itself: maximum riser height of 7-3/4 inches, minimum tread depth of 10 inches, and no more than 3/8 inch of variance between the tallest and shortest riser in a single run. New tread material changes the finished riser height by whatever thickness gets added on top of the old one, so on a remodel we calculate that variance before we ever cut the first tread, not after installation reveals a step that's taller than the one above it. We measure existing tread depth and riser height on-site before ordering material, not from a builder's original plan set, since decades of paint buildup, prior remodels or settling can shift those numbers by a fraction of an inch, enough to matter under the 3/8-inch variance rule.

sections.h2: Matching treads to a new or existing field floor
sections.html:
The tread and the field floor need to read as one continuous material from the top of the stairs to the bottom, even when they're technically different products. We stain-match hardwood and engineered treads to an existing field floor's color, and for LVP or laminate stairs we source tread kits from the same product line as the field floor whenever the manufacturer offers one. Where a manufacturer doesn't make a matching stair nose for their LVP line, and plenty don't, a stained hardwood tread that coordinates with the plank color is the more durable fix than a glued-on vinyl nosing that eventually works loose.

Landings get treated as an extension of the upstairs field floor rather than as another stair tread, so the material transition happens at the base of the top riser, not partway across the landing. On a curved or winder staircase, each tread is a slightly different shape, which is part of why fabrication happens off-site rather than from stock-length boards.

High-gloss finishes look sharp in photos and turn genuinely slippery on a staircase, which is the wrong tradeoff on the most-used stairs in the house. Textured or brushed finishes, stair runners, or a clear anti-slip tread coating all reduce slip risk without changing the look much from a few feet away. We bring this up before finish selection, not after someone's first trip down the stairs in socks. Households with young kids or older pets sometimes ask about carpet runners for cushioning as much as for grip; a runner secured with proper stair rods or adhesive strips works for that, though it does mean vacuuming a strip nobody sees as often as the rest of the house.

Tread fabrication happens off-site, because staircases are almost never perfectly square and each step gets measured individually rather than cut from a single template. Installation happens on-site working up the staircase one tread and riser at a time, so the stairs stay usable through the job. Most full staircases of 14 to 22 steps finish in two days; a small half-flight of 6 to 8 steps can often finish in one. A typical example: a 16-step staircase in a two-story Lakewood Ranch home getting engineered hardwood treads to match new field flooring downstairs. Fabrication takes two to three days once measurements are taken, and installation itself runs a single day once material is ready, with risers painted the following day when they aren't being stained to match. Scheduling around the rest of the household matters too; we sequence a full staircase from the top down so upstairs bedrooms stay reachable by a temporary walkway for as much of the job as possible.

If you're replacing the field floor at the same time, see our hardwood, vinyl plank or laminate pages for that half of the project, or our stair tread cost guide for a full per-step price breakdown. Loose or squeaking treads down the road from the original installation are covered under our two-year workmanship warranty; our floor repair team handles tightening and re-fastening either way.

sections.h2: Stair treads in condos and rental turnovers
sections.html:
A staircase in a two-story rental or a townhome sees the heaviest daily traffic in the unit, which is why we lean toward LVP or laminate treads with a durable factory finish for short-term rental properties rather than a site-finished stain that needs babying for the first week. Glued LVP treads hold up well to rolling suitcases on the nosing, the single spot on any staircase that takes the most abuse.

For condo buildings, stair remodels are almost always interior to the unit rather than the building's common stairwell, so HOA sound-transmission rules that apply to field flooring typically don't apply to a private staircase the same way; it's still worth confirming with the association before assuming that exemption applies to your building. Wellen Park and Parrish stair remodels most often pair with a full downstairs LVP or laminate replacement happening in the same week, since both projects share the same furniture-clearing disruption and it's more efficient to schedule them together.

faqs.q: What nosing projection does Florida code require on stair treads?
faqs.a: Florida Residential Code sets nosing projection between 3/4 inch and 1-1/4 inch on stairs with solid risers. We fabricate every tread inside that range, and it's one of the first things we check on a remodel where the new tread material is a different thickness than what's coming out.

faqs.q: Will new, thicker treads throw my riser heights out of code?
faqs.a: It can, if nobody accounts for it. Florida code caps riser height at 7-3/4 inches and limits the difference between the tallest and shortest riser in a run to 3/8 inch. Adding tread material on top of an existing stringer changes every riser's effective height by that same thickness, so we calculate the new riser heights before cutting the first tread, not after.

faqs.q: Should stair treads be glued down or floated like the field floor?
faqs.a: Glued, not floated, for LVP and laminate treads. A floating plank relies on the planks around it to stay locked in place, which works on an open floor but not on a stair edge with nothing to lock against. We glue every stair tread regardless of material, the same way solid and engineered hardwood treads have always been fastened to the stringer.

faqs.q: How do you make a hardwood or laminate staircase less slippery?
faqs.a: A textured or brushed finish instead of high-gloss is the first fix, since gloss finishes are the most likely to feel slick underfoot. Stair runners or a clear anti-slip tread coating are the other two options we bring up, and we'd rather have that conversation before the finish goes on than after someone slips.
